strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scaling video generation from seconds to minutes under scarce long-form data, with a clear conceptual distinction between temporal extrapolation and spatial interpolation (Fig. 1).

The proposed decoupling of local fidelity and global coherence via a shared long-context encoder with separate Flow Matching and Distribution Matching heads is a sensible architectural response to conflicting objectives, and the ablation in Table 2 supports the utility of the decoupled design.
Uses mode-seeking reverse-KL alignment via DMD/VSD on sliding windows, enabling few-step inference (4 NFE) while attempting to preserve local realism from a short-video teacher.

Quantitative results on VBench-style metrics and a Gemini-based consistency metric show competitive or best overall performance, especially on dynamic degree and imaging quality, and the ablation isolates the contributions of SFT, sliding-window DMD, and dual heads.

Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 4 illustrate the intended failure modes of SFT-only and teacher-only baselines, and the paper correctly notes that AR-based methods can inflate consistency by becoming static or over-saturated.

The method is positioned as orthogonal to causal autoregressive models, which is a useful practical observation and suggests possible combinations with rollout-robust training or context-extension techniques.
The supplementary material provides some implementation and data details, including the sliding-window DMD image-latent reconstruction trick and the Gemini evaluation prompt.
weaknesses: The central claim of scaling to 'minute-scale' videos is not directly supported: experiments generate only 30-second videos, even though the paper repeatedly claims minute-scale generation. No 60-second or longer results are reported, so the fidelity-horizon gap is not convincingly closed at the claimed horizon.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a main-track paper. Key details are missing: exact training hyperparameters (e.g., λ_seg, learning rates, batch sizes, number of updates), teacher checkpoint identity, fake-score estimator training details, data filtering/splitting, compute budget, and random seeds. No code or model release is mentioned.

Baseline comparisons are not compute- or data-matched. Long-context SFT and Mixed-length SFT use 50 NFE, while the proposed method uses 4 NFE; CausVid and Self-Forcing are autoregressive few-step methods trained under different regimes. There are no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests, and no analysis of whether gains are robust across prompts.

The claim 'without requiring any additional short-video data' is misleading because the method depends on a frozen short-video teacher trained on large-scale short-video data. The paper also claims 'no longer need multi-stage training and distillation,' yet the proposed training itself uses DMD/VSD-style distillation plus SFT, which is a form of multi-objective/multi-stage training.

The teacher-student setup is unclear and potentially self-referential: Wan 2.1 1.3B is used as both student and teacher 'whenever involved.' If the student is initialized from the teacher, local fidelity may largely come from initialization rather than the proposed sliding-window alignment, and no cross-teacher or randomly initialized student experiment isolates this effect.

Mathematical and notational inconsistencies hinder understanding and reproduction. Eq. (9) uses v_fake on the full long latent while the teacher term is on a cropped window, creating a dimension/semantic mismatch; Eq. (10)-(13) inconsistently mix x_t^{long}, \hat{x}_t^{long}, L, and K; and it is unclear how a DM head trained mainly through cropped windows reliably generates long videos end-to-end beyond the shared encoder argument.

Evaluation is narrow. VBench-style metrics are short-video oriented and can be gamed by static or slow videos; the paper relies on a single MLLM consistency score, with no FVD, no human study, no long-video-specific benchmark, and no detailed analysis of event/narrative coherence beyond consistency and motion smoothness.

Presentation quality needs improvement: there is a duplicated sentence ('We summarize our key contributions as follows:'), dense related-work sections read as citation lists rather than critical synthesis, figure captions are truncated, and some references are inconsistent or mislabeled.

Limitations and ethics treatment are inadequate. The main paper does not discuss the 30s-vs-minute mismatch, teacher dependence, or compute/data constraints; the impact statement dismisses societal consequences, and there is no discussion of web-scraped video data, copyright/privacy, or deepfake/misinformation risks.

The ablation does not fully isolate whether separate heads are necessary versus simply using gradient stopping or loss weighting on a single head. The reported drop for 'No DDT dual heads' could reflect optimization difficulty rather than a fundamental architectural conflict.

The claim that the DM head inherits local realism from the teacher is plausible, but the paper does not measure how much local fidelity is due to the teacher versus the long-video SFT data or the base model. This weakens the causal interpretation of the main results.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem: the fidelity–horizon trade-off in long video generation, and the framing in Figure 1 (temporal extrapolation ≠ spatial interpolation) is intuitive and well-motivated.

The decoupled design—a shared long-context encoder with separate Flow Matching and Distribution Matching heads—is architecturally sensible, and the ablation (Table 2) does support that the dual-head design matters (the 'No DDT dual heads' row shows the largest drop).

The on-policy sliding-window DMD with image-latent reconstruction to avoid window-boundary semantic mismatch (Sec. C) is a useful practical contribution that could help others implement windowed distillation on modern video VAEs.
The DM head enables few-step (NFE=4) inference without a separate multi-stage distillation pipeline, which is a practical benefit.
The limitations/future-work section is honest and identifies concrete extension directions (causal AR distillation, longer-context positional schemes).
weaknesses: The central empirical claim ('best overall', 'closes the fidelity–horizon gap') is not supported by Table 1. The proposed method does not dominate: CausVid has higher Subject Consistency (0.9736 vs 0.9682), Background Consistency (0.9614 vs 0.9548), and Aesthetic Quality (0.6044 vs 0.5735), and Long-context SFT has higher VLM Consistency (77.28 vs 75.42). No aggregate/composite metric is reported, so the 'best overall' claim rests on cherry-picking favorable columns.

The VLM Consistency numbers are anomalous: AR baselines (CausVid 39.30, Self-Forcing 37.60) are roughly half of all other methods (74–77). A ~2x gap is implausible as a genuine quality difference and suggests the Gemini metric is confounded (e.g., penalizing saturation) rather than measuring what the paper claims. This is hand-waved in Sec. 4.2 ('over-saturated') instead of investigated, undermining a headline metric.

Ablation margins (Table 2) are extremely small (e.g., consistency 0.9615 full vs 0.9604 without sliding-window DMD; motion 0.9685 vs 0.9621). With no variance, seeds, or significance reporting, these differences cannot support strong causal conclusions about individual components.

The 'gradient interference' motivation (Sec. 3.3) is asserted rather than demonstrated. There is no analysis (e.g., gradient conflict measurements, cosine-similarity of gradients) to justify why a single head fails; only the ablation is offered as evidence.

Reproducibility is limited: no hyperparameters (λ_seg, DMD weighting λ(t), fake-score-estimator update schedule/learning rate, number of training steps), no compute budget, and no mention of code/model/data release. The '5 steps' fake-score update and the two-minibatch schedule are described only in prose.

The 'Fast' claim in the title is under-supported: NFE=4 is reported but there is no wall-clock/latency comparison, no ablation over the number of steps, and no analysis of how few-step inference interacts with minute-scale bidirectional generation.

Presentation quality is below standard: a duplicated sentence ('We summarize our key contributions as follows: We summarize our key contributions as follows:'), inconsistent notation (the DM head is written as $D_\psi^{\mathrm{DM}}$ in text/equations but $D_\phi^{\mathrm{DM}}$ in the Figure 2 caption; $\phi,\psi,\theta$ are mixed; Eq. 13 uses $x_t^{\mathrm{long}}$ where $\hat{x}_t^{\mathrm{long}}$ is intended), a broken Eq. 9 layout, and a typo ('Wan 2.1 1.3B'). The related-work section is largely an undifferentiated citation dump with little synthesis.

The methodological contribution is incremental: it combines existing components (DDT decoupled heads, DMD/VSD distillation, sliding-window teacher matching à la LongLive/CausVid). The novelty is the specific combination rather than a new principle, and the paper does not isolate what is genuinely new beyond the ablation.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only a single base model family (Wan 1.3B) is used for the main quantitative comparison, the test set is 200 prompts, and comparisons with strong long-video systems are limited to AR-extrapolation baselines; no comparison to recent bidirectional long-video methods that could directly compete.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper distinguishes temporal extrapolation from spatial interpolation (Fig. 1) and identifies the fidelity-horizon gap in long-video generation.

The proposed decoupled training paradigm is technically sound: a shared long-context encoder with a mean-seeking flow-matching head for long-video SFT and a mode-seeking distribution-matching head for sliding-window reverse-KL teacher alignment (Eqs. 5, 9, 15-18) is a sensible way to combine complementary objectives.
Practical few-step inference: using only the DM head at 4 NFE enables fast long-video synthesis, as shown in Table 1, which is a meaningful efficiency benefit over 50-NFE SFT baselines.

Empirical validation is reasonably thorough: Table 1 shows strong dynamic degree (0.9453) and image quality (0.6982), and Table 2 ablates each component (no DDT dual heads, no sliding-window DMD, no SFT), supporting the design choices.
Qualitative results (Figs. 3-4) illustrate sharper local details and better long-range consistency than SFT-only and teacher-only baselines.

The paper provides useful implementation details in the supplement (data sources, DeepSpeed Ulysses, FastGen, sliding-window DMD adaptation, Gemini evaluation prompt) and includes a limitations/future work section.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited: no code release and many key hyperparameters are missing (learning rate, batch size, training steps, λ_seg, window length L, number of windows, fake-score update frequency, model dimensions). This makes independent reproduction difficult.

Evaluation is narrow: only 200 prompts, 30-second videos, and one base model family (Wan 1.3B/14B). There is no human evaluation, no comparison to other non-autoregressive long-video methods (e.g., SkyReels-V2, HunyuanVideo, LongLive), and no statistical significance testing.

The 'best overall' claim is not fully supported by the table: the method is not best on VLM consistency (75.42 vs. 77.28 for Long-context SFT) or subject consistency (0.9682 vs. 0.9685/0.9689), and improvements over mixed-length SFT are moderate on several metrics.

Technical clarity needs improvement: Eq. (9) inconsistently applies v_fake to the long sequence while u_teacher is windowed; Eq. (14) has a typo (D_b^{FM} instead of D_θ^{FM}); the DM head is supervised only on sliding windows and its long-range behavior relies on the shared encoder, but this is not directly ablated.

Potential confound: gains over SFT baselines may partly stem from access to a strong short-video teacher rather than solely from the decoupled architecture. The ablation 'No DDT dual heads' helps, but teacher capacity/quality is not controlled.

Some claims are overbroad: 'we no longer need multi-stage training and distillation' is confusing because the method uses DMD-style distillation; 'without requiring any additional short-video data' relies on a frozen short-video teacher trained on such data.

Research ethics/data treatment is underdeveloped: the paper uses randomly collected internet videos but does not discuss copyright, privacy, consent, or potential biases in the long-video corpus; the impact statement is generic.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated conceptual decomposition: routing a mean-seeking flow-matching objective to global long-video structure and a mode-seeking reverse-KL objective to local sliding windows is a clean idea that follows directly from the observation that the two objectives have different point-wise optima (conditional mean vs. a high-density mode) and would otherwise interfere on a single head.

The framing in Fig. 1 (temporal extrapolation vs. spatial interpolation) is compelling and correctly identifies why mixed-length 'soup' training is insufficient; this gives the paper a clear, principled problem statement.
The ablation study (Table 2) directly validates each component, showing the largest degradation when the dual-head decoupling is removed, which supports the authors' gradient-interference motivation.

The user study (Table 4) provides meaningful independent evidence: the method is preferred on overall quality and global consistency at both 30s and 60s, and substantially reduces static artifacts relative to rollout baselines.
The few-step inference result (NFE = 4 vs. 50 for SFT baselines) is a genuine and practical efficiency benefit that follows naturally from the DMD-style DM head.
The limitations section is honest, identifying event-level planning and temporal-causality failures rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative table (Table 1) shows only marginal and inconsistent gains: subject consistency (0.9682 vs. 0.9685), motion smoothness (0.9863 vs. 0.9866), and VLM consistency (75.42 vs. 77.28) are all worse than Long-context SFT, while quality/dynamic improvements are small. No error bars or confidence intervals are reported, so the significance of these differences is unclear and the central claim of 'jointly improving' is only weakly supported by automatic metrics.

The long-range consistency part of the central claim is not clearly demonstrated on the main benchmark (parity or worse on consistency metrics); the argument relies heavily on the user study and the 60s stress test.
The 60-second benchmark (Table 3) omits the SFT-only baselines that are the most directly comparable and most important for the fidelity-horizon claim, so the long-horizon evidence is incomplete.

The dismissal of strong baseline results (CausVid, InfinityRoPE, LongLive) as 'over-saturated' or 'conservative' in the Table 1 caption and Fig. 4 is somewhat post-hoc and hand-wavy; it is used to explain away metrics on which baselines do better without quantitative backing.

The core architecture (Decoupled Diffusion Transformer with dual heads) is borrowed from prior work (Wang et al., 2026b); the novelty lies primarily in routing the two objectives to disjoint content axes, which is a somewhat incremental combination of existing DMD/VSD and long-video SFT components.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code, model, or checkpoint release is mentioned, and the pipeline depends on proprietary components (FastGen, specific data curation). The bibliography also contains year mismatches and apparent duplicates (e.g., 'Chen et al., 2024' and 'Guo et al., 2024' entries), indicating sloppy referencing.

Baseline comparability is not fully addressed: autoregressive methods (CausVid, Self-Forcing, LongLive) are compared against a bidirectional model with different sampling regimes and context handling; the paper acknowledges NFE is not comparable for LongLive but does not resolve the broader fairness question.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper articulates the 'fidelity–horizon gap' and makes a crisp argument (Fig. 1) that temporal extrapolation is fundamentally harder than spatial resolution interpolation, which is a useful conceptual contribution.

A sensible architectural decoupling: routing a mean-seeking SFT flow-matching head and a mode-seeking sliding-window distribution-matching head through a shared long-context encoder is a clean way to separate global coherence from local realism, and it yields a genuinely fast (4 NFE) long-video sampler.

The evaluation is relatively broad: it includes VBench-style automatic metrics, a 60-second stress test, a 31-participant user study, and an ablation, plus comparisons against several strong autoregressive/distillation baselines (CausVid, Self-Forcing, InfinityRoPE, LongLive).

The limitations section is honest and specific, identifying failure modes such as misinterpreting compositional temporal instructions and failing to revisit landmarks, and pointing to concrete future directions.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are marginal and sometimes negative relative to the simplest baselines. In Table 1, the method's VLM consistency (75.42) is lower than Long-context SFT (77.28), and its subject consistency (0.9682) is lower than Long-context SFT (0.9685); motion smoothness (0.9863) is essentially tied with Long-context SFT (0.9866). No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, so it is not possible to conclude that the central claim ('closing the fidelity–horizon gap') is supported.

The 'teacher' is the same base model as the student (Wan 2.1 1.3B), so the framing that the short-video teacher supplies 'web-scale diversity' the student lacks is misleading — the student is initialized from the teacher, and the DM head is effectively self-distillation to preserve the base model's local quality. This substantially weakens the novelty narrative.

The theoretical argument that mean-seeking SFT and mode-seeking DMD 'conflict' (Sec. 3.3) is undercut by the shared encoder: both objectives update E_φ (Eq. 16), so the interference is relocated to the encoder rather than eliminated. The paper gives no analysis of why sharing the encoder is safe while sharing a head is not, and the 'No DDT dual heads' ablation alone cannot establish this.

The DM loss only constrains sliding-window marginals (Eq. 5, 9). The joint distribution over non-overlapping windows — the actual object generated at inference — is never constrained, and no window-level fidelity check or joint-distribution validation is provided. The claim that long-range coherence is guaranteed by the shared encoder is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, λ_seg is never given a value, the '5 steps' of fake-score training and the DM-head initialization are vague, and dataset construction ('randomly collected internet videos', filtering) is underspecified.

The ablation (Table 2) uses aggregate metrics (Consistency/Motion/Quality) that are never defined, and the differences are tiny — e.g., removing SFT actually improves 'Motion' (0.9690 vs 0.9685) — so it does not clearly establish the necessity of each component.

Reference and presentation issues: duplicate entries (e.g., Chen et al. 2024 and Guo et al. 2024 appear twice), core building blocks cited as future-dated 2026 works, and the mislabeling 'Sliding Window DMD (Yin et al., 2024b)' — Yin et al. 2024b is the (non-sliding-window) DMD paper, which suggests citation sloppiness.

The human study reports close scores (e.g., Ours 3.68 vs LongLive 3.12) with no significance testing, and the 60-second setting excludes SFT-only baselines, making cross-horizon comparisons inconsistent.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: long-video generation under scarce long-form data, with a clear fidelity-horizon trade-off framing.

The conceptual decomposition is compelling: temporal length is treated as extrapolation rather than spatial interpolation, and local fidelity is decoupled from global coherence via mode-seeking teacher alignment and mean-seeking long-video SFT.

The architecture is technically plausible: a shared long-context encoder with separate Flow Matching and Distribution Matching heads avoids forcing conflicting objectives through a single velocity predictor.

The sliding-window DMD/VSD adaptation to bidirectional long-video models is nontrivial and includes a sensible fix for the teacher's image-latent prefix mismatch by decoding/re-encoding the last frame and masking the reconstructed latent.

The empirical package is broad: 30-second VBench-Long comparisons, a 60-second stress test, human ratings, and component ablations. The method achieves strong dynamic degree, image quality, and VLM consistency, and is competitive on subject/background consistency.
The ablation study supports the main design choices, especially the benefit of decoupled heads and the need for both SFT and sliding-window distribution matching.
Reproducibility is partially addressed: base models, data sources, training hardware, sequence-parallelism setup, implementation repository, evaluation protocol, and Gemini prompt are described.
Limitations are discussed honestly, including failure cases in event-level temporal planning and revisitation.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing components (DDT-style decoupled heads, DMD/VSD, sliding-window distillation, long-video SFT). The main novelty is routing mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives to different content axes, which is useful but not a fundamentally new method.

Evaluation fairness is not fully clean. The main table compares the proposed 4-NFE DM sampler against SFT baselines at 50 NFE, which conflates method quality with sampling-step advantage. The ablation also does not specify the inference head/NFE for ablated variants, so removing components may also remove the few-step sampler. A comparison of the FM head vs. DM head at matched NFE is missing.
The 'fast' claim is not quantified by wall-clock latency, memory, or throughput; NFE alone does not capture the cost of full long-context attention at inference.

VBench-style metrics may not fully capture long-range narrative/event coherence. The method is not best on every metric (e.g., subject/background consistency and aesthetic quality in Table 1), and several margins are small without error bars or significance tests.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a complex method: key hyperparameters such as lambda_seg, learning rates, batch sizes, training steps, window length/stride, number of sampled windows, DMD fake-score update details, and lambda(t) weighting are not reported. No code or model release is mentioned.

Several technical details are ambiguous or inconsistent: Eq. (4) suggests non-overlapping windows despite the 'sliding-window' claim; Eq. (9) uses v_fake on the full long latent while the text describes a window-level fake score estimator; Eqs. (10)-(13) use x_0^long and hat{x}_t^long inconsistently.
The ablation does not clearly isolate head decoupling from loss weighting or from the inference-time sampler, so the conclusion that decoupled heads are essential is only partially supported.
The user study lacks methodological detail: rating scale, confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement, participant compensation, and IRB/consent information are not reported.

Research ethics and broader impact are under-treated. The impact statement is essentially dismissive, and the paper does not discuss risks such as deepfakes, misinformation, copyright, or privacy, despite using randomly collected internet videos and public datasets.

There are minor citation/presentation issues, e.g., 'Sliding Window DMD (Yin et al., 2024b)' likely should point to CausVid (Yin et al., 2025), Eq. (5) uses an odd dotted-q notation, and temporal flickering is mentioned but omitted from Table 1.
